title: WHY WAS RAHAB’S HOUSE BUILT INTO JERICHO’S WALL?
paragraphs:
WHY WAS RAHAB’S HOUSE BUILT INTO JERICHO’S WALL?
She lived in the place everyone trusted for protection. Then the wall fell—and the woman everyone could have condemned became the one God refused to forget.
There is one detail in the story of Rahab that is so easy to read past that most people never stop long enough to feel its weight.
Her house was in the wall.
Not simply near Jericho’s wall.
Not merely somewhere inside the city.
Scripture says:
וַתּוֹרִדֵם בַּחֶבֶל בְּעַד הַחַלּוֹן כִּי בֵיתָהּ בְּקִיר הַחוֹמָה וּבַחוֹמָה הִיא יוֹשָׁבֶת
Vattoridem baḥevel be'ad haḥallon, ki veitah beqir haḥomah, uvaḥomah hi yoshevet.
“Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was in the wall of the fortification, and she was dwelling in the wall.”
—Joshua 2:15
The Hebrew is striking.
בְּקִיר הַחוֹמָה — beqir haḥomah
Literally, “in the wall of the fortification.”
Then Scripture emphasizes it again:
וּבַחוֹמָה הִיא יוֹשָׁבֶת — uvaḥomah hi yoshevet
“And in the wall she was dwelling.”

The text wants you to notice where Rahab lived. Ancient Jewish interpreters noticed it too; Joshua 2:15 became the basis of discussion precisely because her dwelling was understood as being associated with, or actually within, the city wall.
And once you notice it, the story becomes almost unbearable in its beauty.
Because the wall that should have made Rahab vulnerable became the location from which salvation entered her house.
Think about that.
Jericho was facing judgment.
Israel was coming.
Rahab knew it.
The city knew it.
Fear was already spreading before a single wall collapsed.
She told the spies:
יָדַעְתִּי כִּי־נָתַן יְהוָה לָכֶם אֶת־הָאָרֶץ
Yada'ti ki-natan YHWH lakhem et-ha'aretz.
“I know that the LORD has given you the land.”
—Joshua 2:9
Not “I wonder.”
Not “I have heard rumors.”
Yada'ti.
“I know.”
Something had happened inside this woman before anything happened to Jericho’s walls.
Faith had entered.
And that changes everything.
Rahab is introduced in Joshua 2:1 with an uncomfortable word:
זוֹנָה — zonah.
The ordinary Hebrew meaning is a prostitute.

Some later traditions have associated Rahab with an inn or innkeeping, but we should not erase the scandal Scripture itself allows to stand. The Greek New Testament is even more explicit. Hebrews 11:31 calls her Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη — Rhaab hē pornē, “Rahab the prostitute,” and James 2:25 similarly identifies her as Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη.
The Bible does not sanitize her résumé before telling us what grace did with her.
That matters.
Because some of us have spent years trying to edit the parts of our story we are afraid other Christians might discover.
We know how to smile in church.
We know what to post.
We know which Bible verse belongs in the caption.
We know when to say, “God is good.”
But somewhere behind the smile is a room we hope nobody enters.
An addiction.
An affair.
A secret.
A compromise.
A season of rebellion.
A body carrying memories nobody knows about.
A marriage barely surviving.
A private habit contradicting a public testimony.
A past you wish could be deleted.
Rahab’s story begins with Scripture refusing to delete hers.
“Rahab the prostitute.”
And strangely, that is part of what makes the Gospel-shaped trajectory of her life so beautiful.
God is not glorified because Rahab had no scandal.
God is glorified because her scandal did not get the final word.
But there is another question.
Why was her house in Jericho’s wall?
Scripture never directly tells us why Rahab personally came to occupy that particular dwelling. We should be careful not to invent an explanation and call it biblical truth.
What Scripture does tell us is that her house’s position made the events of Joshua 2 possible.
Her house had a window opening through the wall.
That meant two Israelite spies trapped inside an enemy city had an escape route.
Rahab lowered them through that window by a rope.
The place where she lived suddenly became strategically important in God’s unfolding purpose.

Archaeology confirms that ancient Jericho was a heavily fortified Canaanite settlement during portions of the Bronze Age. Excavations have revealed substantial fortification systems involving stone retaining structures, mudbrick defenses, ramparts, and multiple phases of construction. Scholars continue to debate the chronology and how particular archaeological destruction levels should be correlated with the biblical account, so archaeology should not be stretched beyond what it can establish. No responsible reading requires us to pretend that archaeologists have discovered a house and proven, “This was Rahab’s bedroom.”
The inspired text gives us what we actually need.
Her dwelling was associated so intimately with Jericho’s fortification that she could lower the spies through its window to the outside.
And suddenly her address becomes part of the story.
The woman on the edge of the city...
was positioned at the edge of a miracle.
Imagine that night.
Two men disappear through her window.
A rope rubs against the wall.
Rahab watches them descend into darkness.
These men belong to the people whose God is coming against her city.
Everything Rahab has known is behind her.
Everything she has chosen to believe is disappearing into the night in front of her.
And she has been given a command.
Put a scarlet cord in the window.
The Hebrew expression in Joshua 2:18 is:
תִּקְוַת חוּט הַשָּׁנִי — tiqvat ḥut hashani
A cord—or line—of scarlet.
The word תִּקְוָה — tiqvah can carry the sense of a cord in this context and elsewhere means “hope” or “expectation.”
We should be careful here.
Joshua does not explicitly tell us that the author intends the scarlet cord as a direct prophecy of Christ’s blood.
The New Testament does not explicitly make that identification either.
So we should not declare a symbolism Scripture itself does not declare.
But a Christian reader can hardly miss the larger biblical pattern without feeling its resonance.
Judgment is approaching.
A household has received a promise of deliverance.
A visible sign marks the place where those trusting the promise have gathered.
And those who remain within are spared.
It inevitably reminds us of Passover.
Blood on a doorway.
Judgment passing through.
A household sheltered because God had provided the terms of deliverance.
And both stories eventually point our eyes toward the greater deliverance accomplished not through a cord in a window or blood on an Egyptian doorway, but through Jesus Christ Himself.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the announcement that good people can escape judgment.
It is the announcement that guilty people can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus.
That is Rahab territory.
That is Gospel territory.
That is where some of us are standing right now.
Between what we have been...
and what grace is calling us to become.
Then Jericho falls.
Joshua 6 says Israel circles the city according to God’s command.
Trumpets sound.
The people shout.
And the wall collapses.
Now think again about where Rahab lives.
In the wall.
The very thing that gave her house its location was the thing under divine judgment.
Yet before Jericho fell, Rahab had already made her choice.
She had chosen the God of Israel over the gods of Jericho.
Listen to her confession:
כִּי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הוּא אֱלֹהִים בַּשָּׁמַיִם מִמַּעַל וְעַל־הָאָרֶץ מִתָּחַת
“For the LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath.”
—Joshua 2:11
Do you see what happened?
Before Rahab ever left Jericho...
Jericho had begun leaving Rahab.
Her address was still Canaanite.
Her past was still Canaanite.
Her neighbors were still Canaanite.
Her house was physically attached to Jericho’s defenses.
But her faith had changed allegiance.
And perhaps that is exactly where someone reading this is living.
You have not escaped everything yet.
Your circumstances have not changed yet.
The addiction is still calling.
The divorce papers are still sitting there.
The grief is still in the room.
Your family still remembers who you used to be.
Your consequences have not magically disappeared.
Your reputation may not have recovered.
You may still be physically surrounded by the world you are trying to leave spiritually.
Rahab understands.
She trusted God while she was still living in Jericho.
Faith began before relocation.
Then judgment came.
Joshua commanded the two spies:
“Go into the prostitute’s house and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her, as you swore to her.”
They went in.
They brought Rahab out.
Her father.
Her mother.
Her brothers.
Everything belonging to her.
Her family.
The woman whose house had once stood as part of Jericho’s wall crossed from the condemned city into the company of God’s covenant people. Joshua 6:25 says Rahab lived among Israel afterward.
But God was not finished.
Centuries pass.
Kings rise.
Kingdoms fall.
Prophets speak.
Generations are born and buried.
Then Matthew begins telling the story of Jesus Christ.
And there...
inside a genealogy most people rush through...
a familiar name appears.
Ῥαχὰβ — Rahab.
Matthew 1:5 places Rahab in the genealogy leading to David and ultimately to Jesus Christ.
Stop there.
The woman introduced in Joshua as a prostitute appears in Matthew in the ancestral line through which the Messiah enters history.
The woman in the wall became a woman in the genealogy.
Jericho knew her by her occupation.
Scripture remembers her by her faith.
Hebrews 11 places her among examples of faith:
“By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had received the spies with peace.”
James remembers her too, presenting her actions as evidence of living faith.
Her past remained part of the testimony.
But it was no longer the conclusion.
That is grace.
Grace does not pretend the old chapter was never written.
Grace gives the story a new ending.
And that is why Rahab’s story must ultimately bring us to Jesus.
Because Jesus does not merely make embarrassing people respectable.
He saves sinners.
The cross tells the truth about us more brutally than our shame ever could.
Our sin is not a minor defect requiring improvement.
It separates us from a holy God.
We cannot rescue ourselves by becoming religious enough, moral enough, charitable enough, or publicly respectable enough.
We need mercy.
We need forgiveness.
We need reconciliation.
We need a Savior.
And Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we could never perfectly live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds something Rahab discovered long before Bethlehem:
God's mercy can reach a person standing inside a condemned city.
Maybe you have been living inside your own Jericho.
Building walls.
Protecting secrets.
Telling everyone you are fine.
Perhaps you have become so skilled at hiding that nobody knows you are exhausted.
But you know.
And God knows.
Maybe the question is no longer whether God can forgive someone like Rahab.
The question is whether you believe He can forgive someone like you.
He can.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the cross proves that it does.
And not because repentance is unnecessary.
Rahab’s faith changed her allegiance.
Saving faith does not say, “Jesus, bless the Jericho I refuse to leave.”
It says, “Jesus, I surrender.”
Repentance is not paying God back.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can save.
Maybe your scarlet cord moment is now.
Not because repeating a sentence saves you.
Not because commenting on a Facebook post saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But perhaps you need to stop hiding.
And believers who see those words—do not judge them.
Pray for them.
Because the church should be one of the safest places on earth for a Rahab to encounter the truth that leads to repentance and the grace that leads to restoration.
Not merely because sharing helps a page.
It does not.
Not because supporting a ministry earns salvation. It cannot.
Salvation is God's gift through Christ.
But believers have always used their resources to help truthful Gospel ministry continue.
Not out of guilt.
Out of mission.
Because somewhere behind somebody's carefully constructed wall is a person convinced that God would never want them if everyone knew what they had done.
Rahab destroys that lie.
Her story does not teach us that sin is harmless.
It teaches us that grace is greater.
Her story does not tell us everyone automatically escapes judgment.
It tells us that faith takes God seriously enough to change allegiance.
Her story does not end with a prostitute hiding spies in Jericho.
It reaches forward into Hebrews.
Into James.
Into Matthew.
Into the genealogy of Jesus Christ.

And ultimately toward the Savior whose Gospel announces that sinners can become sons and daughters, outsiders can be brought near, shame does not have to become identity, and yesterday does not have authority to write tomorrow.
Maybe that is why the location of Rahab’s house feels so unforgettable.
She lived in a wall everyone thought was strong enough to protect a city.
Then the wall failed.
But the God she trusted did not.
Jericho's wall could not save Rahab.
Her reputation could not save Rahab.
Her courage could not ultimately save Rahab.
Her works demonstrated the reality of her faith, but salvation belonged to the God in whom she placed that faith.
And the same truth reaches us through the completed Gospel today.
Your church attendance cannot save you.
Your Christian posts cannot save you.
Your charitable giving cannot save you.
Your good intentions cannot save you.
Your ability to hide your scandal cannot save you.
Jesus can.
So come out from behind the wall.
Bring the shame.
Bring the memories.
Bring the consequences.
Bring the years you wish you could recover.
Bring the secret nobody knows.
Bring the heart you thought God could never want.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing.
Because the Gospel has never been the story of spotless people climbing their way toward God.
It is the story of a holy God coming down to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Rahab had a window in a wall.
God turned it into an escape route.
Rahab had a past stained by sin.
God turned it into a testimony of faith.
Rahab belonged to a condemned city.
God brought her among His people.
Rahab carried a name associated with scandal.
God placed that name inside the earthly family line leading to Christ.
And perhaps the most beautiful thing about Rahab is that Scripture never needed to pretend she had always been someone else.
Grace was powerful enough to tell the truth.
The wall carrying Rahab's old life fell—but the mercy carrying her future never did.
